ANOTHER KETTLE OF FISH

By: Anina Peens | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
When even our fish are getting hooked on drugs, we have real problems in South Africa

Unique Selling Point:
When dangerously high levels of toxins revolt fish eagles and Cormorants from eating fish, why is fish caught in the Klipvoor dam fed to humans?

Summary:
Now that the majority of Rhino have been either poached, saved or dehorned, South Africa’s natural world is facing another major challenge that few may have seen coming; Fish poaching. Our freshwater dams are being stripped down of its fish species, seemingly by highly organized syndicates controlled by immigrants. And what the consumers are unaware of, is that the fish may cause devastating illness and even death. This while South Africans either work for the syndicates or unknowingly create a lucrative market, keeping the criminals in business.

Further information:
THE STORY
In the Borakalalo national park in the Northwest province, seasoned ranger and wildlife expert, Gift Ramoitheki is fighting to reclaim the once glorious 13 thousand hectares of bushveld and woodlands from the devastating grip of syndicates. Along with his highly trained team of rangers, he has had many successes tracking down criminals and poachers at the Vaalkop dam where he used to be head ranger. Now, Northwest parks moved gift to Borakalalo national park, where things are out of control and the park has literally gone down the drain.
Syndicates poach everything that moves in the park, but the biggest money is in the water of the protected Klipvoor dam. 800 hectares of spectacular waters were once home to hundreds of indigenous fish and bird species. It was one of the largest breeding grounds of fish eagle in the country.
Today, it’s a sad and different picture. Dead fish heap up on the edges of the dam, covered in a thick green mess. And although it seems like a free buffet for the Cormorants and Fish eagles that are left, the fish rot as nothing wants to eat it.
However, despite the obvious danger signs, illegally caught fish from Klipvoor dam is sold for human consumption and criminals are doing lucrative business with unknowing consumers.
Fish are poached by AK47 carrying men, mostly originating from the banks of Lake Tanganyika over 2000 kilometers North. Advanced netting is used to scoop up tons of fish which are sold on to local communities, infiltrates the informal sector in cities and are finally exported across Africa.

BACKGROUND
What will you find if you follow the Apies River in Gauteng from its source to its end?
The answer may shock you.
Over two million people’s sewage waste flows down this river and its now considered one of the dirtiest rivers in the world.
Originating South op Pretoria, it flows through the center of the city and then forms a confluence with the Pienaars river taking with it a mass of human waste from the inner city, Soshonguve, Attridgeville and Pretoria North and then feeds into the Klipvoordam in the Borakolalo national park.
A river has the natural ability to cleanse itself and cleaner water should be found downstream as it flows. But the Apies River is beyond any form of rehabilitation, as the levels of toxins increases downstream. A myriad of toxins are carried down its waters, killing everything that consumes it. Antibiotics, anti-depressants, eyewatering levels of estrogen as well as dangerous metals. This is all due to the collapse of the Rooiwal wastewater works in Pretoria. This is well-known information, that government have been unable to repair and upgrade this vital wastewater works. The department of water and sanitation has partnered with the Tshwane municipality and estimates that the city needs over 4 billion Rand to repair Rooiwal. This while the SIU is in the process of investigating tender fraud within the municipality amounting to over 295 million Rand.
President Ramaphosa visited Rooiwal last year after a cholera outbreak in Hamanskraal. He apologized to the people and admitted government has failed them. Ever since, there has been no sign of immediate plans to fix the system.
And the consequences are getting out of hand. A group of scientists from the University of Stellenbosch started research on the water from Apies and Pienaars river and followed it downstream to Borakolalo. Despite from the fact that the pathologist, working with the team ended up in ICU after dissecting the fish, another strange discovery was made; the water contains such high levels of cocaine and Tik, that the fish are getting addicted to it. The team will continue research in October to establish what the effect is on human consumption of the fish.
Unaware, or careless, the syndicates continue, unaltered distributing fish to surrounding communities. If you follow the fish, you will find informal roadside stores Brits- the closest big town to the park- where women buy the fish, smoke it and sell it.
The syndicate’s infiltration into the community is concerning and the park’s rangers are now teaming up with provincial police. Raids are increasing to three times a week but it’s a losing battle as the syndicates just changes location across the banks of the over 800 hectares of the Klipvoordam.



Extra Budget Items:
We will need 3 shooting days for this story: We will go fishing and take the fish for analysis. then we need a day to shoot the raids on the Syndicates and then another day for interviews and analysis. We will also need R&D budget to pay for the lab costs for analysing the fish that we will be catching on Wednesday (25 September).

KETTLE OF FISH DRAFT SCRIPT 3

OPENING

VO
Twice a week, these farmers and local businessmen wake up at 2 o’clock in the morning. They get together here, at the Klipvoor dam in the Borakolalo national park between Brits and Thabazimbi in the North West.

UPSOUND

VO
Together with park management and rangers, they’re clearing illegal gill nets - trying to drive out the poachers stripping the dam of its fish.

SOURCE: BORAKOLALO
CLIP: 0293
THEMBA
05:22:24:44
We are under siege. everyday they are coming in putting up nets.

VO
But as day breaks, a strange picture unfolds. Scores of dead fish wash up on the shore…something is lurking under the murky surface of the dam. And it's killing the fish…
PAUSE
UPSOUND OF WATER?
VO
Now scientists are researching what exactly is going on and what they’ve found in the water is unnerving.

PART 1

VO
Our journey begins 80 km upstream, just outside Pretoria. This is the Apies River, a major tributary of the Klipvoor Dam. Two years ago, a cholera outbreak in Hammanskraal made international headlines.

Corruption, fraud and lack of maintenance had caused the Rooiwal Wastewater works to collapse. Government hung its head in shame.

UPSOUND: RAMAPHOSA ‘ GOVERNMENT HAS FAILED THE PEOPLE’

VO

Two years later, nothing has changed.

VO
SOURCE: PETER DAY 1
CO234
The smell is overpowering its unbelievable, and every single day, thousands of liters of sewage are going straight into the river. This hasn’t been treated, its literally going straight into the river. No wonder there’s nothing that lives there. Oof! [coughs]

PAUSE

VO
But cholera was only one result of the defunct waste water works. The collapse of Rooiwal has caused a chain reaction along the entire Apies River, from where the effluent enters the Apies river in Pretoria to the Klipvoor dam, 80 kilometres downstream.


SUPER@ DR CHRISTOFF TRUTER: WATER SCIENTIST
SOURCE: BORAKOLALO
CLIP: 0354
10:18:53:23
We were wondering what was happening further north downstream as you follow the river.

VO
Dr Christoff Truter is leading the research with a group of scientists from the universities of Stellenboch, Limpopo and Onderstepoort.

SUPER@ DR CHRISTOFF TRUTER: WATER SCIENTIST
SOURCE: BORAKOLALO
CLIP: 0354
10:19:15:23
There’s a point where, if the river is impacted too much, it cannot clean itself. So the question was, can this heavily polluted Apiesriver, clean itself if we track it downstream and where does it go?

VO
We decide to see for ourselves what life can survive in water so polluted.

UPSOUND
MAC GETTING GEARED FOR THE TRIP
Ready!

UPSOUND ANDRE
We are going to make use of an electro-fisher to collect the fish.

VO
Veteran water expert, Andre Hoffman takes us into the river, just below the Rooiwal wastewater works.

UPSOUND
MAC/ANDRE HOFFMANN GETTING DRESSED IN THEIR WATER GEAR

VO
The extra protection is because pollution levels are so high here, we’re advised not to even breathe freely.

SUPER@ ANDRE HOFFMAN: WATER EXPERT
SOURCE: PETER CAM DAY 1
CLIP 0186
10:41:38:07
I’ve been working on the Jukskei which is very bad also, but this is much worse.

VO
We find no fish… not even catfish, a hardened species… In fact, we find no animal life.

SUPER@ ANDRE HOFFMAN: WATER EXPERT
SOURCE: PETER CAM DAY 1
CLIP 0206
11:27:06:04
VO: We move further downstream, about 8 kilometres from the sewage works.

MAC: So maybe here there may be a bit more luck?
Andre: Yes, it might have recovered a little.

VO
Here, a beautiful wedding venue once sprawled on the river bank. Now it’s deserted… we don’t spot a single insect.

SUPER@ ANDRE HOFFMAN: WATER EXPERT
SOURCE: PETER CAM DAY 1
CLIP 0206
If you remove the sewage works or get the sewage works to release proper cleaned water, then it should recover within two years.
MAC: Two years?
11:28:06:34
Yes. But to recover to what it was will take 50 to 70 years.
Mac: 50 to 70 years!
Andre: actually, it will never recover to what is was… I don’t see any movement of fish, I don’t see any invertebrates moving.
MAC: And by invertebrates you mean things like…
Andre: Midge larvae, dragonfly larvae, stuff like that, yes.

PAUSE

VO
A flow of raw sewage destroys not only life in the water, but livelihoods on its banks.

SUPER@THEUNS VOGEL: FARMER
SOURCE: KETTLE OF FISH DAY 1
CLIP: C0141
08:55:32:34
Met die probleme met die ekoli en die gehalte van die water is ons deur die markte van Pretoria en Johannesburg gestop om enigsins enige produkte te lewer.

VO
Theuns Vogel’s farming dreams are over. A couple of years ago, Rooiwal’s dam walls caved in and sludge flooded Theuns’s farm.

SUPER@THEUNS VOGEL: FARMER
SOURCE: KETTLE OF FISH DAY 1
CLIP: C0141
08:55:52:04
Daai rou grys sludge het veroorsaak dat my skade op my grond so groot geraak het dat ek nou nie meer groenmielies plant nie want die blare is fisies swart gekleur. Dit het totaal my hele boerdery vernietig.

VO
Theuns has no choice but to give up farming, and no one will buy his land. Like some of his elderly, unemployed neighbours, Theuns will soon depend on a state social grant to put food on the table.

SUPER@THEUNS VOGEL: FARMER
SOURCE: KETTLE OF FISH DAY 1
CLIP: C0141
09:06:19:12
Ons kan niks doen nie. Ons is heeltemal basies gekortwiek om enige iets te doen. Jy weet, ek is al 71, ek wil ook graag dalk n bietjie aftree of rus of iets anderste doen maar nou sit ek hier vasgevang. Hulle hou my ‘n gevang op my eie grond.

PAUSE/TRANSITION

VO
On the banks of the dam, Dr Truter and his team have set up a makeshift lab. They’re dissecting specimens to determine whether the river has cleaned itself on its 80km journey from Rooiwal.

UPSOUND: Pull over you’ll see the slimy threads. That's an indication that the gills are irritated.

VO
Dr Johan Steyl, a pathologist from Onderstepoort, says the fish are in terrible health: low oxygen levels and high levels of pollutants in the water have left them vulnerable to parasites, like these ones, found in the brain of a carp.

SUPER@ DR CHRISTOFF TRUTER: WATER SCIENTIST
SOURCE: BORAKOLALO
CLIP: 0354
10:19:43:18
This is probably the most eutrophic dam I’ve experienced in my life, eutrophic in a sense of continuous algae blooms.
10:21:43:18
The dominant species in this bloom is Microcystis, so it’s a cyanobacteria, its known to produce cyanotoxins

VO
Dr Truter is talking about a blue green algae that flourishes in the presence of sewage - and produces a potent natural poison.

VO
Water tests also raise serious concerns.

SUPER@ DR CHRISTOFF TRUTER: WATER SCIENTIST
SOURCE: BORAKOLALO
CLIP: 0354
10:26:11:17
pharmaceuticals, antibiotics, antidepressants, anti-fungals, killing yeast and fungi, and also ARV, antiretroviral drugs which are used by AIDS patients.

VO
As these chemicals wash into the dam with untreated wastewater, what is the effect on the ecosystem in and around the dam?

SUPER@ DR CHRISTOFF TRUTER: WATER SCIENTIST
SOURCE: BORAKOLALO
CLIP: 0354
10:32:56:17
We’re collecting fish here and we’re analysing the muscle itself to see whether we can find [...] some of the antibiotics or other drugs and whether that would pose both a risk in humans, but we are very interested in animals, the risk to animals. In this system you’ve got fish eagles and larger animals, there’s crocodiles eating the fish, so they’re also at risk.

VO
And that’s not all: the water contains illicit drugs…

SUPER@ DR CHRISTOFF TRUTER: WATER SCIENTIST
SOURCE: BORAKOLALO
CLIP: 0354
10:27:18:38
Methamphetamine was one of the interesting ones, which is Tik.

VO
Tik: a cheap, highly addictive drug and one of the most-abused substances in South Africa. It’s in the water at such high levels that the fish themselves can become addicted.

10:27:28:35
We did find one microgram per litre of Tik, of methamphetamine, in the Apies river. That was quite interesting because another study that was published by a British group shows that at that level of methamphetamine, trout fish would become addicted to that drug.
MAC: the fish could get addicted to the drug itself, fish swimming in that kind of water?
“Yes, there are studies that show behaviour studies, they select visits to the place where there is high drug levels.

VO
And that’s not where it ends. Levels of human hormones like oestrogen are off the charts: 130 times as much as the international guideline. So high, it changes the biology of the fish.

SUPER@ DR CHRISTOFF TRUTER: WATER SCIENTIST
SOURCE: BORAKOLALO
CLIP: 0354
10:30:57:17
That can feminise fish, so if you have male fish, they could be feminized, and it could affect their reproduction.

VO

What no one knows is the effect this pollution has on the people who depend on the dam to supply their water and food.

SUPER@ DR CHRISTOFF TRUTER: WATER SCIENTIST
SOURCE: BORAKOLALO
CLIP: 0354
10:33:34:48
These are communities living 80 kilometres downstream of the pollution source, they had absolutely nothing to do with the problem but they’re sitting with the legacy of what’s going on upstream and they are eating this fish and drinking this water.

SOURCE: BORAKOLALO
CLIP: 0293
THEMBA
05:25:03:02
It ends up in the street, black-markets, if you go to Pretoria, Mabupane station, they are selling it everywhere, they are not even hiding, they are selling it public.

VO
While the scientists are busy in their makeshift lab, rangers and farmers are pulling net after net out of the dam.

SOURCE: BORAKOLALO
CLIP: 0309
THEMBA
05:55:57:07
As you can see the fishes are dying, this net has been here for a day or two.

SOURCE: BORAKOLALO
CLIP: 0317
THEMBA
06:29:10:21
They collect the fishes from the dam, they put them into 125-liter buckets. If you carry one bucket it's 120 to 150. Then if they sell it to the black market, the biggest carp they can sell for R250 to R300 each. Showing that they’re making good money out of this. That’s why they never stop. Even how hard we try, they never give up.

VO
Every day, bakkie loads of fish are shipped from the park. Criminals are caught but never prosecuted, allowing a lucrative business to flourish off the back of unsuspecting consumers.

…Vital ecosystems and habitats are collapsing…

…all as a result of government’s inability to repair Rooiwal wastewater works.


























PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO
Farmers on the Apies River near Pretoria are at their wits’ end.
SUPER@THEUNS VOGEL: FARMER
SOURCE: KETTLE OF FISH DAY 1
CLIP: C0141
08:53:57:08
Ons kannie verder hier aangaan nie want ons boerdery word benadeel ons grond word besoedel, ondergrond, gesondheid, jy kan se, enige ding wat n mens aan kan dink, ons mense regte totaal word vernietig.
VO
The collapse of Rooiwal wastewater works is causing devastation that can be seen for kilometers between Gauteng and the North West Province.
SUPER@THEUNS VOGEL: FARMER
SOURCE: KETTLE OF FISH DAY 1
CLIP: C0141
08:58:29:06
Ek noem dit ‘n man-made disaster wat eintlik ‘n kriminele klag is.

PROMO 2
VO
While farmers bear the brunt of the collapse of Rooiwal wastewater works…
SUPER@THEUNS VOGEL: FARMER
SOURCE: KETTLE OF FISH DAY 1
CLIP: C0141
09:06:19:12
Ons kan niks doen nie. Ons is heeltemal basies gekortwiek om enige iets te doen. Jy weet, ek is 71, ek wil ook graag dalk n bietjie aftree of rus of iets anders doen maar nou sit ek hier vasgevang. Hulle hou my ‘n gevang op my eie grond.
VO
The devastation to the river’s ecosystem will not easily be reversed.

PROMO 3
VO
When scientists follow the Apies River from its source to the Klipvoordam…
SUPER@ DR CHRISTOFF TRUTER: WATER SCIENTIST
SOURCE: BORAKOLALO
CLIP: 0354
10:18:53:23
We were wondering what was happening further north downstream as you follow the river.
VO
What they find in the water is shocking.
SUPER@ DR CHRISTOFF TRUTER: WATER SCIENTIST
SOURCE: BORAKOLALO
CLIP: 0354
10:32:56:17
We’re collecting fish here and were analysing the muscle itself to see if we can find illicit drugs or some of the antibiotics or other drugs and whether that would pose both a risk in humans

PROMO 4
VO
Poachers are stripping the Klipvoor dam of its fish .

SOURCE: BORAKOLALO
CLIP: 0293
THEMBA
05:25:03:02
It ends up in the street, black-markets, if you go to Pretoria, Mabupane station, they are selling it everywhere, they are not even hiding, they are selling it public.

VO
But are these fish safe for human consumption?

VO Now scientists are researching what exactly is going on and what they’ve found in the water is unnerving. PART 1 VO Our journey begins 80 km upstream, just outside Pretoria. This is the Apies River, a major tributary of the Klipvoor Dam. Two years ago, a cholera outbreak in Hammanskraal made international headlines. Corruption, fraud and lack of maintenance had caused the Rooiwal Wastewater works to collapse. Government hung its head in shame. UPSOUND: RAMAPHOSA ‘ GOVERNMENT HAS FAILED THE PEOPLE’ VO Two years later, nothing has changed. VO SOURCE: PETER DAY 1 CO234 The smell is overpowering its unbelievable, and every single day, thousands of liters of sewage are going straight into the river. The collapse of Rooiwal has caused a chain reaction along the entire Apies River, from where the effluent enters the Apies river in Pretoria to the Klipvoor dam, 80 kilometres downstream. UPSOUND MAC GETTING GEARED FOR THE TRIP Ready! UPSOUND ANDRE We are going to make use of an electro-fisher to collect the fish. VO Veteran water expert, Andre Hoffman takes us into the river, just below the Rooiwal wastewater works. SUPER@ DR CHRISTOFF TRUTER: WATER SCIENTIST SOURCE: BORAKOLALO CLIP: 0354 10:26:11:17 pharmaceuticals, antibiotics, antidepressants, anti-fungals, killing yeast and fungi, and also ARV, antiretroviral drugs which are used by AIDS patients. SUPER@ DR CHRISTOFF TRUTER: WATER SCIENTIST SOURCE: BORAKOLALO CLIP: 0354 10:30:57:17 That can feminise fish, so if you have male fish, they could be feminized, and it could affect their reproduction. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): When even our fish are getting hooked on drugs, we have real problems in South Africa
metadata.Unique Selling Point: When dangerously high levels of toxins revolt fish eagles and Cormorants from eating fish, why is fish caught in the Klipvoor dam fed to humans?
metadata.Summary: Now that the majority of Rhino have been either poached, saved or dehorned, South Africa’s natural world is facing another major challenge that few may have seen coming; Fish poaching. Our freshwater dams are being stripped down of its fish species, seemingly by highly organized syndicates controlled by immigrants. And what the consumers are unaware of, is that the fish may cause devastating illness and even death. This while South Africans either work for the syndicates or unknowingly create a lucrative market, keeping the criminals in business.
metadata.Further information: THE STORY In the Borakalalo national park in the Northwest province, seasoned ranger and wildlife expert, Gift Ramoitheki is fighting to reclaim the once glorious 13 thousand hectares of bushveld and woodlands from the devastating grip of syndicates. Along with his highly trained team of rangers, he has had many successes tracking down criminals and poachers at the Vaalkop dam where he used to be head ranger. Now, Northwest parks moved gift to Borakalalo national park, where things are out of control and the park has literally gone down the drain. Syndicates poach everything that moves in the park, but the biggest money is in the water of the protected Klipvoor dam. 800 hectares of spectacular waters were once home to hundreds of indigenous fish and bird species. It was one of the largest breeding grounds of fish eagle in the country. Today, it’s a sad and different picture. Dead fish heap up on the edges of the dam, covered in a thick green mess. And although it seems like a free buffet for the Cormorants and Fish eagles that are left, the fish rot as nothing wants to eat it. However, despite the obvious danger signs, illegally caught fish from Klipvoor dam is sold for human consumption and criminals are doing lucrative business with unknowing consumers. Fish are poached by AK47 carrying men, mostly originating from the banks of Lake Tanganyika over 2000 kilometers North. Advanced netting is used to scoop up tons of fish which are sold on to local communities, infiltrates the informal sector in cities and are finally exported across Africa. BACKGROUND What will you find if you follow the Apies River in Gauteng from its source to its end? The answer may shock you. Over two million people’s sewage waste flows down this river and its now considered one of the dirtiest rivers in the world. Originating South op Pretoria, it flows through the center of the city and then forms a confluence with the Pienaars river taking with it a mass of human waste from the inner city, Soshonguve, Attridgeville and Pretoria North and then feeds into the Klipvoordam in the Borakolalo national park. A river has the natural ability to cleanse itself and cleaner water should be found downstream as it flows. But the Apies River is beyond any form of rehabilitation, as the levels of toxins increases downstream. A myriad of toxins are carried down its waters, killing everything that consumes it. Antibiotics, anti-depressants, eyewatering levels of estrogen as well as dangerous metals. This is all due to the collapse of the Rooiwal wastewater works in Pretoria. This is well-known information, that government have been unable to repair and upgrade this vital wastewater works. The department of water and sanitation has partnered with the Tshwane municipality and estimates that the city needs over 4 billion Rand to repair Rooiwal. This while the SIU is in the process of investigating tender fraud within the municipality amounting to over 295 million Rand. President Ramaphosa visited Rooiwal last year after a cholera outbreak in Hamanskraal. He apologized to the people and admitted government has failed them. Ever since, there has been no sign of immediate plans to fix the system. And the consequences are getting out of hand. A group of scientists from the University of Stellenbosch started research on the water from Apies and Pienaars river and followed it downstream to Borakolalo. Despite from the fact that the pathologist, working with the team ended up in ICU after dissecting the fish, another strange discovery was made; the water contains such high levels of cocaine and Tik, that the fish are getting addicted to it. The team will continue research in October to establish what the effect is on human consumption of the fish. Unaware, or careless, the syndicates continue, unaltered distributing fish to surrounding communities. If you follow the fish, you will find informal roadside stores Brits- the closest big town to the park- where women buy the fish, smoke it and sell it. The syndicate’s infiltration into the community is concerning and the park’s rangers are now teaming up with provincial police. Raids are increasing to three times a week but it’s a losing battle as the syndicates just changes location across the banks of the over 800 hectares of the Klipvoordam.
